reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare low-grade malignant bone tumour with a striking predilection for the mid-diaphysis of the tibia, typically in adolescents and young adults.
It is biphasic, combining epithelial islands with an osteofibrous stroma, and the epithelial cells are reliably cytokeratin positive.
It sits on a spectrum with osteofibrous dysplasia and osteofibrous-dysplasia-like adamantinoma, which can complicate diagnosis on small samples.
Anterior tibial swelling, often with a long indolent history and sometimes anterior bowing of the leg, is the usual presentation.
Radiographs classically show multiple eccentric, lytic, cortically based lesions with sclerotic margins, giving a soap-bubble appearance along the diaphysis.
The tumour is essentially resistant to both radiotherapy and chemotherapy, so wide en bloc resection with clear margins is the definitive treatment.
Intralesional curettage is inadequate and associated with high local recurrence.
Late local recurrence and metastasis, chiefly to the lungs and regional lymph nodes, can occur many years after treatment, mandating prolonged follow-up.
reference.pathophysiology: Adamantinoma is thought to arise from epithelial elements within bone, and the tumour shows a biphasic pattern in which nests, cords or gland-like islands of epithelial cells are set within a fibrous or osteofibrous stroma. The epithelial component expresses cytokeratins and is regarded as the neoplastic driver, while the osteofibrous background resembles osteofibrous dysplasia. The close morphological and clinical overlap between osteofibrous dysplasia, osteofibrous-dysplasia-like adamantinoma and classic adamantinoma supports a shared histogenetic continuum, with progressive expansion of the epithelial component marking the more overtly malignant end. The tibial diaphyseal cortex is the characteristic site, and slow local growth with the potential for delayed metastatic spread reflects its low-grade biology.
additionalInvestigations: plain radiographs of the tibia demonstrating cortical lytic and sclerotic change
MRI to delineate intramedullary and soft-tissue extent
CT to assess cortical destruction and lesion architecture
representative open biopsy with adequate sampling of epithelial foci
staging CT of the thorax for pulmonary metastases
redFlags: rapid increase in size or pain in a long-standing tibial lesion
soft-tissue mass extending beyond the cortex
new pulmonary or nodal lesions on staging
reference.prognosis: With adequate wide resection the outlook is generally good, but the tumour is prone to late local recurrence and delayed metastasis, so long-term surveillance is essential and outcome worsens with inadequate initial surgery.
pitfalls: misclassifying the tumour as benign osteofibrous or fibrous dysplasia on a small biopsy
treating with intralesional curettage, which leads to recurrence
expecting a response to radiotherapy or chemotherapy
curtailing follow-up too early given the risk of late metastasis
underestimating intramedullary spread and resecting with inadequate margins
